en: The Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator is lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin Record.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī; when the time for the meal arrived, he entered the city.
While he was begging for alms,
there was in the city of Vaiśālī a Licchavi named Vīrasena (translated into Chinese as Yǒngjūn, "Brave Army").
Just as a deva might enjoy himself in the company of celestial maidens, this prince likewise enjoyed himself with his court ladies atop a pavilion, becoming deeply immersed in sensual desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing that sound of music with his all-encompassing wisdom, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I know that this person, who is greedy for the pleasures of the five desires, will not live long before his life comes to an end."
"Seven days from now, he shall abandon such kinsmen and pleasures; his death is certain. Ānanda!
If such a person were not to renounce sensual delights and leave the household life, at the end of his life he might fall into hell."
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instructions upon the crown of his head and desiring to benefit this prince, went next to his residence.
When the prince heard that Ānanda was outside, he immediately came out to pay his respects; out of reverent mindfulness, he invited Ānanda to enter and sit.
Not long after he had sat down, the prince, with a heart of profound reverence, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Excellent! A true and good friend has come; now is precisely the right time."
Seeing you now, I am leaping with joy and gladness.
Your name is "Joy"; you should now teach and inform me of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, so as to bring me joy.
At that time, the prince made this request three times.
Ānanda, desiring to bring about great benefit, remained silent and spoke no word.
The prince spoke again:
"The great seer Vidyāha-muni benefits all sentient beings.
For what reason do you harbor resentment and remain silent without saying anything?
We do not see even the slightest word from you!"
Then the third teacher—the upholder of the Buddha’s Dharma-treasury and benefactor of the world—said with a sorrowful countenance:
"Listen well now! Seven days from now, you shall reach the end of your life."
If you cannot awaken to these pleasures of the five desires and do not go forth from the household life, at the end of your life you will likely fall into hell.
The Buddha, the Omniscient One, speaks with truthful words and makes this prediction concerning you.
"Just as fire burns objects, it never fails to ignite them.
Reflect upon this carefully!
When the prince heard these words, he was filled with great anxiety and fear; distressed and unhappy, he accepted Ānanda’s instruction.
"I shall renounce the household life; let me first enjoy pleasure for another six days, and on the seventh day, I will bid farewell to my family and kin and certainly go forth into homelessness."
Ānanda agreed to this.
On the seventh day, out of fear of birth and death, he requested the Buddha for ordination; the Buddha immediately granted his permission.
Having observed the pure precepts for one day and one night, he then passed away.
When the incense burning was finished, the Venerable Ānanda, together with his retinue, went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu Vīraśreṇya has now passed away; where has his consciousness been reborn?"

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Omniscient One, with a Brahma-like voice surpassing the sounds of thunder, drums, and the kalaviṅka bird, addressed Ānanda with eight qualities of speech:
“This bhikṣu Vairaṇa, out of fear of birth-and-death and the sufferings of hell, has renounced desire and left the household life.”

Because he maintained the pure precepts for one day and one night, after passing away from this world, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King. There, he indulged his heart in the pleasures of the five desires; greedily enjoying these five desires, he took delight together with various celestial maidens for a lifespan of five hundred years.

After five hundred years had passed, his life ended and he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as a son of Śakra, where he fully experienced the supreme celestial pleasures of the five desires, indulging with exquisite celestial maidens for a thousand years at will.

When his lifespan ended, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven as a prince of the Ābhāsvara devas; there he indulged at will in the divine forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures, experiencing the pleasures of the mind and desires.

Having lived for two thousand celestial years, his life ended and he was reborn as a prince in the Tuṣita Heaven. There he indulged his heart in the pleasures of the five desires; yet, though his eyes beheld forms and desired them, his mind remained naturally content. He constantly discoursed on the Dharma, liberation, and wisdom, living for the full lifespan of that heaven.

After four thousand years had passed, his life came to an end and he was reborn in the Heaven of Sovereignty as a prince of the gods. There he enjoyed various sublime pleasures of the five senses, sporting at will among the celestial maidens for eight thousand years.
After eight thousand years had passed, his life ended and he was reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations as a prince of the gods.
The sensual pleasures within this sixth heaven are such that they cannot be equaled by those in the five lower heavens.
Having been born therein, they experience the most exquisite pleasure, a treasury of all delights.
While experiencing this bliss, their minds become utterly intoxicated.
They fully enjoy these various sublime and superior pleasures for sixteen thousand years.
Experiencing such bliss, he will travel back and forth among the six heavens of the desire realm for seven cycles.

Because this Vīraśāna went forth as a renunciant for a single day and night, for twenty kalpas he shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; he will always be born among gods and humans, receiving natural blessings.
In his final birth among humans, he was born into a wealthy and prosperous family, fully endowed with riches and precious treasures.

When his youth had passed and his faculties were matured, fearing the calamities of birth, old age, sickness, and death, he grew weary of the world and left the household life. Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he practiced with diligent effort, maintained the four dignified postures, and constantly practiced right mindfulness. Contemplating the five aggregates as suffering, empty, and non-self, and understanding the causal conditions of phenomena, he became a Pratyekabuddha named Vidyuddeva.

At that time, he emitted a great radiance, whereby many humans and devas gave rise to roots of goodness, causing all living beings to plant the causes and conditions for liberation through the three vehicles.
At that time, Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Suppose there were someone who allowed another person to leave the household life;..."
If there is one who goes forth into homelessness, and another provides whatever they require, how much merit will that person gain?
Furthermore, if someone destroys another's causal conditions for going forth, what karmic retribution for their offense will they receive?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will fully explain this to me!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If you were to ask me about this matter for a full hundred years, even with my inexhaustible wisdom, were I to speak extensively for you throughout those hundred years—excepting the time spent on food and drink—I still could not exhaustively describe the merits of this person.”
Such a person will be constantly reborn among gods and humans, always becoming a king and experiencing the pleasures of gods and humans.

If one causes someone to go forth as a renunciant within this Dharma of the śramaṇas, or further assists in providing the conditions for their renunciation, they will constantly experience happiness within the cycle of birth and death.
Even if I were to speak of its merit for a full hundred years, it could not be exhausted. Therefore, Ānanda!
Even if you were to question me for the remainder of your life for a full hundred years, and I were to speak of these merits until my parinirvāṇa, I still could not finish.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is anyone who destroys another's causes and conditions for leaving the household life, they have effectively plundered an inexhaustible treasury of virtuous wealth and merit, and have ruined the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the cause of nirvāṇa."
If there are those who wish to destroy the causes and conditions for leaving the household life, they should carefully examine such matters. Why is this?
Because due to these karmic offenses, one will fall into hell, remaining perpetually blind and sightless, and undergoing the most extreme suffering.
If they are born as animals, they will likewise always be blind from birth;
if they are born among the hungry ghosts, they will likewise always be blind from birth.
They shall remain in the sufferings of these three evil realms for a long time before finally attaining liberation.
If you are born as a human being, you will be blind from the moment you take conception within your mother’s womb.

Even if you were to inquire about this meaning for a hundred years, and I were to explain the retribution for this sin for a hundred years with my inexhaustible wisdom, it still could not be fully exhausted.
Among those in the four states of existence, I do not predict that such a person—who is born blind—will ever have a time of liberation.
Why is this? It is entirely because they have disparaged the life of renunciation.

"Or, having accomplished boundless merit, because they have destroyed such wholesome causes and conditions, they undergo immeasurable transgressions; due to obstructing their renunciation, within this mirror of pure wisdom, for the sake of the various wholesome dharmas of liberation,"
If one sees someone who has left the household life to cultivate pure precepts and proceed toward the state of liberation, yet destroys that person’s renunciation by creating obstacles for them;
because of these causes and conditions, one will be born blind from birth and shall not see Nirvana, due to having disparaged the life of renunciation.
One who constantly contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, such as ignorance and the rest, ought to attain liberation;

yet, because they destroy the eye of wisdom in others and obstruct the eye of wisdom that arises from the conditions of renunciation, they remain perpetually blind and sightless from birth to birth, unable to see the three realms due to the obstacles that hinder their renunciation.
One who has left the household life should perceive the five aggregates and the twenty views of self, thereby entering the right path of humanity;
yet because they destroy the causes for leaving the household life and ruin right view, they will be born perpetually blind and fail to see the right path.
One who has left the household life should perceive the collection of all dharmas as the abode of wholesome dharmas, and should contemplate the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
because they destroy the wholesome causes and conditions for leaving the household life, they will be born perpetually blind and unable to behold the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Because one has gone forth, one should possess the appearance of a śramaṇa as well as the observance of the precepts, serving as a pure field of merit to plant the causes for the Buddha-way;

yet by destroying the state of going forth, one cuts off all hope within the wholesome dharmas, and due to these sinful conditions, one shall be perpetually blind in every birth because of having defiled the state of going forth.
One who has left the household life should skillfully observe that all body and mind are suffering, impermanent, non-self, and impure;
to obstruct another’s renunciation and create difficulties for them is to destroy this eye.

Because this eye is destroyed, one does not see the four paths, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path that lead to the city of Nirvāṇa.

Due to these karmic conditions of sin, one will always be born blind, such that one does not even see the pure, wholesome dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which lead toward the city of Nirvāṇa.

"Therefore, a person of wisdom who knows that those who have left the household life ought to accomplish such wholesome dharmas should not destroy the causes and conditions for these wholesome dharmas, thereby incurring such a transgression."

Whoever destroys such causes and conditions for the right view of another who has gone forth as a śramaṇa will never be able to see the city of nirvāṇa; wherever they are born, they shall always be blind.
"Furthermore, if there were a person who, for the duration of a hundred kalpas, went forth as a monastic in another land and practiced pure precepts;

and if there were another person here in this Jambudvīpa who, having gone forth and maintained the precepts for even one day and night, or even for a mere moment, attained the purity of renunciation—then that former person’s hundred kalpas of going forth and maintaining the precepts would not equal even a sixteenth part of this latter person’s merit."

"If there is perversion such that one commits sexual misconduct with sisters or daughters, or in improper places, forcibly giving rise to stinginess and jealousy, the retribution for such offenses therein shall be beyond measure."
If there is a person who correctly contemplates with the resolve to leave the household life, desiring to abandon all evils;

and if another person should destroy this person's conditions for leaving the household life, preventing their vow from being fulfilled, the causal conditions of that sin will increase beyond the former by a hundredfold for a further hundred kalpas.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Vīraśreṇya has planted roots of goodness and shall be born into a noble station to receive blessings and joy; did he also perform virtuous deeds in past lives?”
"Is it only by virtue of the merit of going forth for a single day and night today that one receives such an amount of blessings?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should not contemplate past causes and conditions!"

Because of this pure renunciation for one day and one night, by virtue of these roots of goodness, he will receive blessings seven times among the six heavens of the desire realm and constantly experience the worldly pleasures of birth and death for twenty kalpas.

Finally, among human beings, he was born into a family of merit and happiness; when his youth had passed and his faculties were matured, out of fear of birth, old age, sickness, death, and suffering, he left the household life, observed the precepts, and became a Pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I shall now speak a parable; you should listen well!

Suppose the four continents—the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, the western continent of Aparagoyānī, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru—were filled with arhats as densely as a grove of rice, hemp, or bamboo."

Suppose there were a person who, for the full span of a hundred years, devoted their heart and mind to providing these arhats with clothing, food and drink, medicine for illness and weakness, and dwellings with bedding; and even after their parinirvāṇa, they might erect stupas and temples, making offerings of various precious gems, flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music, hanging jeweled bells, sprinkling scented water, and praising them with various verses.

The merit obtained from such acts—if compared to the merit gained by someone who, for the sake of parinirvāṇa, leaves the household life to receive the precepts and practices them for even a single day and night—the former does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the latter.
For these reasons, sons of good family, you should go forth from the household life and cultivate the pure precepts.
Sons of good family!

Those who require merit, those who seek the wholesome Dharma, and those who would personally receive the Dharma should not create obstacles to the causes and conditions for going forth; rather, they should diligently employ skillful means to encourage and assist them so that it may be accomplished.
At that time, when the great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, there was none who did not grow weary of the world, renounce the household life, and uphold the precepts.

Some attained the stage of *srotāpanna* up to *arhat*; some planted the roots of goodness for *pratyekabuddhahood*; and some resolved their minds upon unexcelled *bodhicitta*. All were filled with great joy, and they received and practiced the teaching with the highest reverence.
The Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home Spoken by the Buddha
